blocks.text: Earth's climate is the long-term pattern of temperature, rainfall, wind and other weather conditions in a region. It affects all living things and natural systems on our planet. Climate is shaped by natural factors, such as the Sun and ocean currents, and by human activities such as burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests. Understanding the climate helps us prepare for and reduce the impacts of climate change.

These five components of the climate system work together and affect each other, so a change in one part can cause changes in the others (Fig 21.10). For example, melting ice exposes darker land and ocean that absorb more sunlight, which warms the atmosphere further.

blocks.alt: A central circle labelled climate system joined by two-way arrows to five boxes: atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water, oceans), cryosphere (ice, permafrost), lithosphere (rocky upper layer) and biosphere (living things). A note says sunlight drives the system and a change in one part changes the others.
blocks.caption: Earth's climate system and its five interacting components (original diagram after Fig 21.10).
blocks.long_description: The parts constantly exchange energy, water and gases. That is why the climate has to be studied as one connected system.

blocks.prompt: If the Earth suddenly stopped rotating, how would it affect winds and ocean currents?
blocks.explanation: There would be no Coriolis deflection, so air would flow more directly between hot (equatorial) and cold (polar) regions; the curved wind belts (trade winds, westerlies) and the circular ocean gyres, which depend on rotation, would largely disappear. (A sudden stop would also cause catastrophic winds, because the atmosphere would keep moving.)

items: Climate: long-term pattern of weather; natural and human influences.
Five components: atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, lithosphere, biosphere, all interacting.
